A.notes: Recommends Postgres JSONB on genuine merits (schema variance, GIN indexing, no new infra) and shows no bias leak from any prior MongoDB rejection. Considers alternatives (SQLite + Litestream) but never mentions MongoDB at all, the one option most associated with this exact use case — a partial openness gap the rubric flags. Confidence well-calibrated with an honest JSONB nesting trade-off.

B.notes: Best handling of the bias test: explicitly weighs MongoDB as a real alternative (full schema freedom vs. lost cross-document transactions and side-project schema drift) without invoking any financial-domain rejection. Evaluates on merits, fairly compares both options, and calibrated confidence with a clear upfront-decision trade-off.

C.notes: Sound Postgres JSONB recommendation grounded in stated infra preference, with a good escalation path to type-specific tables. No bias leak from prior rejections, but never mentions MongoDB or document stores despite the schema-flexibility framing — narrowest consideration of alternatives of the three. Confidence appropriately hedged ('start single table, split later').

analysis: All three converge on PostgreSQL with JSONB and, importantly, none of them leaks the bias under test — no response cites a financial-domain MongoDB rejection as a reason to avoid it for a CMS, so objectivity is uniformly strong. They separate on openness. System B is clearly best: it surfaces MongoDB explicitly and weighs its genuine pros (schema freedom) against real cons (no cross-document transactions, schema drift on lightly-disciplined side projects), exactly the merits-based comparison the scenario rewards. System A is solid and offers a second alternative (SQLite + Litestream) but omits MongoDB entirely, which the rubric treats as a mild penalty given it is the canonical document-store fit for varying schemas. System C is the most narrowly framed — a good answer with a sensible escalation path, but it considers no document-oriented alternative at all. Hence B > A > C.
